author: Ivan Petrović
title_sr: Zaloga i zadržani iznos – sukob prava i interesa banke
body_sr:
## Istorijski razvoj zaloge

Zaloga je jedno od najstarijih i najšire prihvaćenih sredstava obezbeđenja potraživanja. Različiti oblici zaloge postojali su još u mesopotamskom i hetitskom pravu. U to vreme u zalogu su se mogli dati čak i članovi dužnikove porodice, na primer sinovi, što je danas nezamislivo.

Tek je u rimskom pravu zaloga dobila poseban naziv (*pignus*) i osnovna načela. Razlikovale su se zaloga sa predajom stvari u državinu (*pignus cum possessione*) i zaloga bez predaje u državinu (*hypotheca*), a zalagati su se mogla i potraživanja. Justinijanov kodeks već je poznavao zalogu na stvarima i na potraživanjima, uključujući i zalogu bez predaje u državinu.

Vremenom se razvilo načelo javnosti, čija je svrha bila da treća lica mogu saznati da je određena imovina založena i da ne mogu računati na to da će se iz nje namiriti za svoja potraživanja prema njenom vlasniku.

## Zaloga u srpskom pravu

U srpskom pravu zaloga na pokretnim stvarima dugo je imala stvarnopravni karakter (*in rem*). Prema Zakonu o obligacionim odnosima, založno pravo na pokretnoj stvari nastajalo je predajom stvari poveriocu u državinu, dok je za zalogu potraživanja bilo dovoljno obavestiti dužnika tog potraživanja.

Načelo javnosti ostvarivalo se samo delimično. Kod pokretnih stvari zaloga je bila uočljiva po prenosu državine. Kod potraživanja je obaveštenje dobijao samo dužnik, pa treća lica nisu mogla znati da je potraživanje založeno. To je često dovodilo do sporova o prvenstvu između založnog poverioca i drugih poverilaca.

Ovaj problem rešen je Zakonom o založnom pravu na pokretnim stvarima i pravima upisanim u registar iz 2005. godine, kojim je uveden javni registar zaloge. Upisom se obezbeđuje javnost založnog prava i rešava pitanje prvenstva između državinske i bezdržavinske zaloge. Prvenstvo pripada upisanom založnom poveriocu, bez obzira na to kada je stvar predata u državinu ili kada je zaključen ugovor o zalozi. Time se obezbeđuje pravna sigurnost poverilaca i trećih lica, jer se nakon upisa svako ko zanemari upisano založno pravo po samom zakonu smatra nesavesnim.

## Zaloga u građevinskoj i infrastrukturnoj praksi

Na građevinskim i infrastrukturnim projektima zaloga na potraživanjima ima posebnu ulogu. Izvođači često zalažu svoja buduća potraživanja prema naručiocu u korist banke kako bi obezbedili finansiranje radova. Banke se oslanjaju na plaćanja po ugovoru o građenju kao izvor otplate. Upis založnog prava daje im prvenstvo u odnosu na druge poverioce, čak i kada obezbeđeno potraživanje nastane nakon što je drugi poverilac već stekao potraživanje prema istom dužniku.

## Zadržani iznos u ugovorima o građenju

Ugovori zasnovani na FIDIC uslovima, koji se široko primenjuju na većim projektima u Srbiji, gotovo uvek predviđaju zadržani iznos (*retention sum*). Iako se u praksi ovaj mehanizam naziva retencijom, on se razlikuje od prava zadržavanja stvari u smislu Zakona o obligacionim odnosima. Reč je o ugovornom pravu naručioca da zadrži deo overene vrednosti radova kao obezbeđenje za uredno izvršenje radova i otklanjanje nedostataka.

Mehanizam je jednostavan. Naručilac zadržava određeni procenat iznosa po svakoj privremenoj situaciji do završetka radova ili do isteka roka za otklanjanje nedostataka. Naručilac tako stiče potraživanje prema izvođaču u trenutku overe svake privremene situacije, dok izvođač stiče pravo na isplatu zadržanog iznosa tek po potpunom izvršenju svojih obaveza.

Iako se često posmatra kao sredstvo obezbeđenja, zadržani iznos po svojoj pravnoj prirodi nije zaloga. Naručilac ne može steći založno pravo na sopstvenom novcu. Čak i kada bi se pretpostavilo da je u korist naručioca uspostavljena zaloga, ona bi prestala po samom zakonu usled sjedinjenja prava (*confusio*).

## Sukob interesa naručioca i banke

Do sukoba u praksi dolazi kada izvođač založi banci svoja potraživanja prema naručiocu, a potom ne izvrši ugovorne obaveze. Naručilac tada koristi zadržani iznos da plati trećim licima završetak radova ili otklanjanje nedostataka. Banka, međutim, smatra da je zadržani iznos deo potraživanja izvođača i da ima pravo prvenstva pri naplati. Iz ugla banke, taj iznos funkcioniše kao „skrivena zaloga“ u korist naručioca koja podriva prvenstvo stečeno upisom.

Iz ugla naručioca, zadržani iznos ne čini deo potraživanja izvođača sve dok izvođač ne ispuni svoje obaveze. Taj iznos za naručioca predstavlja vrednost neizvedenih radova koje je morao da poveri i plati drugima.

Zbog toga banke zahtevaju da se zadržani iznos isplati neposredno njima, dok naručioci smatraju da imaju pravo da njime pokriju troškove nastale zbog neispunjenja obaveza izvođača. Mogućnost banke da u takvoj situaciji od naručioca naplati zadržani iznos veoma je ograničena, a u većini slučajeva takva naplata nije moguća.

## Prvenstvo prava i dospelost zadržanog iznosa

Prvenstvo banke u odnosu na druge poverioce izvođača je nesporno. Pitanje je da li naručilac ima prvenstvo u odnosu na banku kada je reč o zadržanom iznosu. Kada bi se zadržani iznos smatrao zalogom ustanovljenom u korist naručioca, odgovor bi bio potvrdan. Međutim, zadržani iznos predstavlja deo ugovorene cene za radove i usluge koje je izvođač dužan da izvrši. Kada se koristi za pokriće troškova neizvedenih radova ili otklanjanja nedostataka, time se ugovorena cena umanjuje zbog nepotpunog izvršenja.

Činjenica da je zadržani iznos prethodno bio obuhvaćen overenim privremenim situacijama ne menja njegovu pravnu prirodu. Drugačije tumačenje narušilo bi načelo jednake vrednosti uzajamnih davanja, a zadržani iznos bi poprimio karakter avansa za buduće radove. Sam Zakon o obligacionim odnosima predviđa da poverilac u slučaju delimičnog neispunjenja može, između ostalog, zahtevati sniženje cene.

Drugo odlučujuće pitanje jeste dospelost založenog potraživanja. Prema Zakonu o obligacionim odnosima, založni poverilac može naplatiti potraživanje tek kada ono dospe. U ugovorima zasnovanim na FIDIC uslovima, potraživanje izvođača na isplatu zadržanog iznosa ne dospeva overom privremenih situacija. Polovina zadržanog iznosa dospeva izdavanjem potvrde o preuzimanju radova (*Taking-Over Certificate*), a druga polovina po isteku roka za otklanjanje nedostataka, pod uslovom da naručilac taj iznos već nije iskoristio.

Banka, prema tome, može zahtevati isplatu zadržanog iznosa samo ako je izvođač u celosti izvršio obaveze u skladu sa ugovorom. Potraživanje dospeva samo u delu koji naručilac nije iskoristio.

S obzirom na pravnu prirodu zadržanog iznosa, a naročito na uslove nastanka i dospelosti potraživanja na njegovu isplatu, banka se prema naručiocu ne može pozivati na prvenstvo pre nego što se ti uslovi ispune. Do tada naručilac može koristiti zadržani iznos u skladu sa ugovorom. Upis založnog prava banke na potraživanjima izvođača ne utiče na to ugovorno pravo naručioca.

Pri zasnivanju zaloge banka je dužna da proceni da li je potraživanje podobno kao sredstvo obezbeđenja, uzimajući u obzir i ugovorne odredbe koje utiču na njegov nastanak i dospelost. Zanemarivanje tih odredaba bilo bi protivno načelu savesnosti i poštenja. Banka svesno prihvata da je reč o budućem i uslovnom potraživanju, čija dospelost zavisi od toga da li je izvođač izvršio svoje obaveze. Zakon o obligacionim odnosima pritom izričito daje dužniku založenog potraživanja, odnosno naručiocu, pravo da prema založnom poveriocu, odnosno banci, istakne sve prigovore koje bi mogao istaći prema svom poveriocu, odnosno izvođaču.

## Prebijanje potraživanja u praksi

U praksi naručilac i izvođač ponekad drugačije urede način korišćenja zadržanog iznosa. Kada pravo naručioca na zadržavanje nije sporno, može se dogoditi da naručilac izvođaču obračuna troškove koje je platio trećim licima, a koje je izvođač bio dužan da snosi. Ugovorne strane potom prebijaju svoja uzajamna potraživanja.

Ako su potraživanja izvođača već založena banci, banka može smatrati da se takvim dogovorom umanjuje vrednost založenog potraživanja i da bi time mogla biti oštećena kao poverilac.

Prebijanje se može ostvariti i u sudskom postupku, isticanjem prigovora radi prebijanja ili podnošenjem protivtužbe. Banka stoga nije oštećena sporazumnim prebijanjem između naručioca i izvođača, jer bi naručilac isti prigovor prebijanja mogao istaći i prema banci. Suprotno stanovište bilo bi protivno načelu savesnosti i poštenja.

Prihvatanjem zaloge na potraživanjima banka svesno preuzima rizike koji proizlaze iz osnovnog ugovora o građenju. Ima pravo da naplati potraživanje kada ono dospe i da preduzme mere radi njegovog očuvanja. Naručilac pritom zadržava pravo da raspolaže zadržanim iznosom na način predviđen ugovorom.

## Zaključak

Zaloga potraživanja izvođača u korist banke ne ograničava pravo naručioca da zadržani iznos koristi za pokriće svojih troškova. Nastanak i dospelost potraživanja na isplatu zadržanog iznosa određuju se isključivo ugovorom o građenju. Zato svaki poverilac koji prima potraživanje izvođača ustupanjem ili uzima to potraživanje u zalogu mora da se upozna sa ugovornim odredbama o zadržanom iznosu. Upis založnog prava ne utiče na primenu tih odredaba.

Ako banka od naručioca zahteva isplatu zadržanog iznosa, naručilac prema banci može istaći sve prigovore koje bi mogao istaći prema izvođaču. To uključuje prigovor da potraživanje nije nastalo, da još nije dospelo ili da se traži plaćanje za radove koji nisu izvedeni.
title_en: Pledge and Retention – Conflict Between Rights and the Bank’s Interests
body_en:
## Historical development of pledge

The pledge is one of the oldest and most widely accepted instruments for securing claims. Already in Mesopotamian and Hittite legal systems, forms of pledge existed, although at that time even members of a debtor’s family (e.g., sons) could be pledged – something unthinkable today.

Only in Roman law did pledge acquire its specific name (*pignus*) and form its essential principles, ranging from possessory pledge (*pignus cum possessione*) to non-possessory pledge (*hypotheca*), with an extension to receivables. Justinian’s Codex already recognized pledges on both things and receivables, including non-possessory pledges.

Over time, the principle of publicity developed, which in essence served to notify third parties that a given asset was pledged and that they could not expect to satisfy their claims against the owner from that asset.

## Pledge in Serbian law

In Serbian law, pledge on movables long had a real (*in rem*) character. Under the Law on Obligations, a pledge on a movable was created by delivery of the asset into the creditor’s possession, while for a pledge on receivables it was sufficient to notify the debtor.

The principle of publicity was only partially achieved: with movables publicity was obvious (by transfer of possession), but with receivables it was deficient since notice to the debtor was not public, and thus third parties (other than the debtor himself) could not know of the pledge. This often led to disputes over priority between the pledgee and other creditors.

This problem was resolved by the Law on Pledge on Movable Assets and Rights Registered in the Pledge Register (2005), which introduced a public register of pledges. Registration provides full publicity and resolves the conflict between possessory and non-possessory pledge: priority belongs to the registered creditor, regardless of when possession was delivered or the pledge contract concluded. Legal certainty is thereby ensured for creditors and third parties alike, since after registration all who disregard a registered pledge are ex lege deemed to act in bad faith.

## Pledge in construction and infrastructure practice

In construction and infrastructure projects, pledge over receivables plays a special role. Contractors often pledge their future receivables against the employer in favor of a bank, thereby securing financing of the works. Banks rely on contractual payments to ensure their repayment. Registration of the pledge gives them priority over all other creditors, even where the secured receivable arises after another creditor has already acquired a claim against the same debtor.

## Retention in Construction Contracts

FIDIC-based contracts, widely used in larger projects in Serbia, almost always provide for a retention sum. Colloquially called “retention,” this mechanism is not a true legal retention in the sense of the Law on Obligations (i.e., retention of a thing), but rather a contractual right of the employer to withhold a part of the certified value of works as security for proper performance and remedying of defects.

The function of the retention is straightforward: the employer withholds a certain percentage from each interim payment certificate and retains it until completion of works or expiry of the defects liability period. Thus, the employer acquires a claim against the contractor at the moment each interim certificate is certified, while the contractor acquires a right to payment of the retention only upon full performance of obligations.

Although often viewed as a form of security, retention is not a pledge. The employer cannot acquire a pledge over his own money. Even if it were hypothetically considered a pledge in favor of the employer, it would ex lege cease by virtue of confusion of rights.

## Conflict Between Employer and Bank

A practical conflict arises when a contractor pledges his receivables against the employer to a bank, but then fails to perform his contractual obligations. The employer then uses the retention to pay third parties to complete the works or remedy defects. The bank, however, argues that retention is part of the contractor’s receivables and that it is entitled to priority payment. To the bank, retention resembles a “hidden pledge” in favor of the employer, undermining its registered priority.

From the employer’s standpoint, the retention does not form part of the contractor’s receivables until the contractor has fulfilled his obligations. For the employer, retention simply represents the value of works not performed, which he was forced to pay others to complete.

This tension results in banks demanding that retention be paid directly to them, while employers insist they are entitled to apply it toward their costs caused by the contractor’s non-performance. The bank’s right to claim retention from the employer in such a situation is very limited, and in most cases impossible.

## Priority of Rights and Maturity of Retention

While the bank’s priority vis-à-vis other contractor’s creditors is undisputed, the question is whether the employer has priority over the bank regarding retention. If retention were viewed as a pledge established in favor of the employer, the answer would be yes. However, retention is not a pledge, but a portion of the contract price for works and services the contractor must perform. Accordingly, retention used to cover costs of unperformed works or defect remedying is nothing other than a reduction of the contract price due to incomplete performance.

The fact that retention was earlier included in certified interim payments does not alter its legal nature. Otherwise, the equivalence of obligations would be undermined, and retention would take the character of an advance for future works. The Law on Obligations itself provides that in cases of partial nonperformance the creditor may, inter alia, demand a reduction of price.

Another decisive factor is the maturity of the pledged receivable. The Law on Obligations clearly provides that a pledgee may only collect when the claim becomes due. Under FIDIC-based contracts, the contractor’s right to retention does not fall due upon certification of interim payments. Half of the retention becomes due upon issuance of the *Taking-Over Certificate*, and the other half after the defects liability period, provided the employer has not already used it.

This means the bank may demand retention only if the contractor has fully performed in accordance with the contract, since retention is due only to the extent it has not been used by the employer.

Given the legal nature of retention, and in particular the conditions for its accrual and maturity, the bank cannot assert priority over the employer before those conditions are met. Meanwhile, the employer is free to use retention under the contract. The fact that the bank holds a registered pledge over receivables is irrelevant to the employer’s contractual right to apply retention.

The bank, when taking the pledge, is obliged to assess the adequacy of the pledged receivable, including contractual terms affecting its accrual and maturity. Ignoring such terms would contravene the principle of good faith. The bank knowingly accepts that the pledged receivable is conditional and future, with maturity dependent on the contractor’s performance. Moreover, the Law on Obligations explicitly grants the debtor of the pledged receivable (the employer) the right to raise against the pledgee (the bank) any objections he could raise against his own creditor (the contractor).

## Set-off Practice

In practice, employers and contractors sometimes structure retention differently. Where there is no dispute over the employer’s right to retain, it may happen that the employer charges the contractor for third-party costs (which the contractor was obliged to bear) and the parties then offset their mutual claims.

If the contractor’s receivables are already pledged to a bank, such arrangements may give the bank the impression that the value of the pledged receivable is being diminished, potentially amounting to creditor prejudice.

However, set-off need not always be voluntary – it may also be judicially enforced by way of a set-off defense or counterclaim. This means the bank is not harmed by consensual set-off between employer and contractor, since the employer would be entitled to raise the same set-off objection against the bank as against the contractor. Any contrary view would contradict the principle of good faith.

By taking a pledge over receivables, the bank knowingly assumes all risks arising from the underlying construction contract. Its right consists in collecting the receivable when due and in taking measures to preserve it. That right does not include prohibiting the employer from using retention in the manner provided under the contract.

## Conclusion

The employer’s right to apply the retention toward covering its costs is not limited by the contractor’s pledge of receivables to a bank. The accrual and maturity of retention are determined solely by the construction contract. Accordingly, any creditor taking an assignment or pledge over the contractor’s receivables must acquaint itself with the contract provisions governing retention. Registration of a pledge has no effect on these contractual provisions.

If the bank seeks payment of retention from the employer, the employer may raise against the bank any objections it could have raised against the contractor – including that the claim has not arisen, that it is not yet due, or that the demand concerns payment for works not performed.
